summary_sentence: For example, standing at the shore with eyes 1.8 m up, a ship 20 km away hides its lowest 18.2 m below the horizon — hull and waterline gone, masts and superstructure still showing.
quick_answer: The Hidden Height by Earth Curvature Calculator works out how much of a distant object is hidden below the horizon for an observer at a given height. Enter your eye height and the object's distance and read the hidden amount — why ships vanish hull-first.

Eyes at 1.8 m: horizon 4.79 km away. A ship at 10 km has only its bottom 2.1 m hidden — nearly all of it shows. At 30 km the hidden part is 49.9 m: everything below a 16-storey line is gone.

popular_table.title: Hidden height by distance (observer eye 1.8 m, no refraction)
popular_table.intro: Computed as (D − horizon)² ⁄ 2R beyond the observer's horizon.
popular_table.note: Standard atmospheric refraction bends the view slightly and cuts these figures by roughly a seventh on an average day; temperature inversions can cut far more, which is why distant coasts sometimes loom impossibly complete.

faq: Why does the hidden part grow so fast?
It follows the square of the distance beyond your horizon — double the extra distance, quadruple the hidden height. The curve is gentle nearby and ruthless far away.
Does the object's own height matter?
Only by comparison: the visible part is the object's height minus the hidden height. A 200 m tower at 30 km shows its top ~150 m to a beach observer.
Optics magnify the visible part; they cannot see through the planet. The hidden height is identical — only the detail in what remains changes.
This page's headline figures are geometric; its method note shows the standard-refraction version (effective radius 7⁄6 R), which trims the 20 km example from 18.2 m to about 15.6 m.
